title: A Pack of Cards
tagline: A shuffled deck may be in an order no one has ever seen. Fifty-two cards, fifty-two pictures, and a way to hold them all.
card: Why a shuffled deck is one of a kind, and how to turn each of the 52 cards into a picture and walk through a whole pack.
goal: you will learn a system that gives each of the 52 cards its own picture, use it to memorise a short run of cards, and see how champions go further.

left_off.q: What are the five steps for remembering a name?
left_off.a: Hear it, say it, find one feature, turn the name into a picture, join them. Then review.

left_off.q: Why should your feature choice be kind and neutral?
left_off.a: The pictures are for your own memory; choosing a neutral or admirable feature keeps the method respectful.

left_off.q: When should you review new names?
left_off.a: The same evening, then again after a few days.

story.heading: An order no one has ever seen

text: It is a rainy Sunday and a family is playing cards. Someone shuffles the deck, seven times as they were taught, and puts it in the middle of the table. The cards are no longer in any order a person could name. There is no Ace of Spades first, no King of Hearts at the end. It is a jumble.

Here is something curious. A pack has fifty-two cards, and the number of ways to arrange fifty-two things is fifty-two times fifty-one times fifty and so on all the way down to one. That number begins with eight and has sixty-eight digits. It is so large that a properly shuffled deck is almost certainly in an order that has never existed before, and will never exist again.

check.q: Why is a properly shuffled deck almost certainly unique?
check.a: The number of possible orders of 52 cards is astronomically large, so the chance that anyone has had the same order before is tiny.

parts.talk: Is it more surprising to you that a deck is unique, or that someone can learn that unique order? Why?

text: And yet a person can look at a shuffled deck and learn the whole order. People do it as a hobby and in competitions. They do not do it by repeating seven of hearts, queen of clubs, three of diamonds over and over. A card is a poor thing to remember: the same red and black marks, the same faces, fifty-two almost alike.

What they do is turn each card into a picture, and put the pictures in order along a route. In competitions the best of them learn a pack in less than thirteen seconds. The method is the one you already have.

check.q: How do people learn the order of a pack?
check.a: They give each card its own picture and place the pictures along a route of places.

parts.talk: Would you like to learn a deck? What would you use it for?

text: To do this you need a fixed list of fifty-two pictures, one for each card, so that you never have to decide. The seven of hearts is always the same scene. In this lesson you will learn a simple system, and see how champions make it faster.

Fifty-two pictures sounds like a lot. But there is a pattern. Each suit is a family of thirteen, so you learn four families, not fifty-two separate things. You will build this system one suit at a time, and by the end of the room you will be able to run through a short hand.

check.q: Why does the card system use a fixed list of pictures?
check.a: So the same card is always the same picture and you never have to decide again.

parts.talk: What pattern would you use to give 52 cards 52 pictures? Think of suits as groups.

words.m: to mix up the cards. She shuffled the deck.
one of the four groups of cards: hearts, diamonds, clubs and spades.
the value of a card: ace, two to ten, jack, queen, king.
to put things into groups. Categorise the cards by suit.
the only one of its kind.
the city where a country's government is based.

source: The number of orders of a 52-card pack is 52! (about 8 × 10<sup>67</sup>).

method.x: Give each suit a category and each rank a member of that category. One easy category is capital cities: each suit is a region, each rank is a city.
Each city then becomes a vivid scene you can see: London is Big Ben and a red bus; Tokyo is neon and Mount Fuji; Cairo is the pyramids and a camel.

items.x: Say its suit and rank in your head: seven of hearts.

items.h: Make the scene big and moving.
items.x: You stand in a crowded Ankara market, with the smell of bread and the call to prayer.
Put the scene at the next place on your route.
One picture per card, one place per picture, in order.

method.title: The seven of hearts
lines: You stand at the foot of a glowing white mausoleum on a hill, with a blue sky and a hot wind. Flags snap above you and crowds climb a long avenue of steps.
At place 3 of your route, as the hall of a house.
method.pic: A white mausoleum on a hill in a hot wind, flags snapping, crowds climbing the steps: that is Ankara, so that is 7♥.

method.x: Champions do not use one picture per card. They give every card a person (or a person with an action and an object, like PAO), and then take two or three cards at a time: the first card gives the person, the second the action, the third the object. A pack of 52 then needs only about 17 scenes, and a scene takes a couple of seconds to build. This is how a whole pack can be learned in under a minute.

suit = a region.
rank = a city.
a fixed picture for
each of the 52.
Start small. Learn the clubs this week, then the other suits. The system only works through repetition; once it is automatic you will see the picture the moment you see the card.
Say the thirteen clubs from the ace to the king in order, and describe one scene.

try.title: Which city?
try.prompt: Use the table. Match each card to its city.

try.title: Seven of hearts
try.prompt: Make your own scene for 7♥ (Ankara). Use the senses: what do you see, hear, smell?
try.model: A hot, dry hill under a blue sky; a white marble mausoleum glows in the sun; flags are cracking in the wind; you smell grilled bread; a loudspeaker calls across the city.
checks: I used at least two senses.
It is clearly Ankara (or the city I chose).

try.title: Three cards in a row
try.prompt: Make scenes for 2 of Clubs (Paris), 8 of Hearts (Manila) and A of Spades (Cairo) and put them in three places of your palace.
try.model: Place 1: a giant glass pyramid beside the Seine, with a baker handing you a baguette taller than you (Paris). Place 2: a bright jeepney painted pink, crammed with chickens, pushes through the crowded street (Manila). Place 3: the pyramids glow at dusk and a camel is eating your map (Cairo).
checks: Each card has a distinct scene.
Each scene is at its own place.
They are different from each other.

items.s: In our system each suit is a ___ and each rank is a city.

try.q: Why does a champion take two or three cards at a time?
opts: Fewer scenes means a faster pack: a pack of 52 becomes about 17 scenes
try.why: Combining cards into person-action-object scenes cuts the pictures to a third.

try.title: Run the clubs
try.prompt: Say the clubs from ace to king aloud, with a word or two for each scene.

quiz.q: What is the suit that stands for Europe?
How many scenes does a champion need for a whole pack?
quiz.why: Three cards per scene: person, action, object.

quiz.q: Why must the same card always be the same picture?
opts: So you never have to decide again
quiz.why: A fixed picture makes the system automatic.

quiz.q: What city is the 3 of Diamonds?
quiz.why: Diamonds: A Washington, 2 Mexico City, 3 Ottawa.

challenge.title: Memory challenge: eight cards
challenge.intro: Eight cards drawn at random. Turn each into its city scene and place it at your palace. Type the cards back in order, like 'King of Clubs'.
challenge.study: King of Clubs = Amsterdam. 2 of Hearts = Bangkok. 9 of Spades = Addis Ababa...

look_back.q: What is the first thing to do when you hear a name?
look_back.a: Hear it properly, and ask the person to repeat it if you are unsure.

look_back.q: Which number system holds six digits in one scene?
In PAO, which pair gives the action?
What is the method of loci?
look_back.a: Using places in a fixed route to store pictures in order.

give each card a fixed picture from a system.
